job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Jamal Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I'm at my uncle's electronics repair shop in Nottingham, behind the counter, fixing phones and old hi-fi gear for forty pounds a day. I live with my parents and my grandmother. I finished an electronic engineering degree in June with a pass. My final project was a cheap water-level sensor for farm troughs, and a farmer near Newark tried two of them for a month. Afternoons I send applications and watch videos about circuit design.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the shop teach you that a lecture doesn't?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I haven't done an internship. Everyone says it matters, and they're right, but the shop felt like real work to me. My uncle says one day it could be mine. I'm not sure I want that, because I'd like to see how a big firm runs before I decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because I like it when things stay clear. I'd say nothing's changed, we still need people who can fix things. At church on Sunday somebody would ask what I think, and I'd say don't get distracted by the noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it'd mean the job hunt goes on as it is. I want a proper engineering job at a firm that makes something, like sensors or power equipment, and I don't have the internships. There's a decent number of openings around Nottingham, and I have the shop to fall back on, so I'm not frightened. I'd like to prove I can do it somewhere that isn't family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to ten firms a month and visit two trade fairs where small electronics firms have stalls. I'd bring my water-level sensor and a one-page sheet about the farmer's trial. I'd also ask my uncle to let me do some design jobs, like a custom controller for a customer. I'd use an AI model sometimes for datasheet questions, and check every number against the datasheet itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled and a bit impatient. I want my own start, not one handed to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you want to prove it somewhere that isn't family. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From my father, who worked his way up in a bus garage with no help from anyone. My father says a man should earn a place. If I take the shop job without trying elsewhere, I'd always wonder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the farmer say about your sensor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He said it worked, but the battery died after three weeks and he'd pay more for one that lasted a season. I went home and rewrote the power part. That was the best feedback I've had.

I'd say, don't get distracted by the noise.
think: I want a proper **engineering job** at a firm that makes something real.
I'd like to prove I can do it somewhere that **isn't family**.

Check datasheet questions with an AI model and confirm numbers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably fair. Software will do lots of the paperwork and design checking, and hardware will carry on more slowly. I'd tell my cousins to learn a skill you can't do from a chair. I'd say it respectfully, because some of them sit at desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the circuit design side gets squeezed, because a tool can draft a layout and run the checks. The testing, repairing and building bits stay human for longer. I'd be a junior who needs real hands-on experience, and that's exactly what the shop gave me. So I'm in a stronger place than some course mates who only did the screen part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim at test and production engineering roles where hands matter, and at firms that build equipment for farms or the grid. I'd try an AI tool for routine design checks, once I've seen two engineers use it. I'd also ask my uncle to let me sell repair contracts to local shops. And I'd save 300 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. It's the kind of feeling you get before a match you think you can win but haven't yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see two engineers use it. What would you look for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether they check its work, and whether their boss expects it. If it makes them lazy, I'm out. If it makes them faster and they still check, then I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'sell repair contracts to local shops' mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small shops have cameras, tills and signs that break. I'd offer a yearly deal of 150 pounds, where I check everything twice a year. It's steady income, and it keeps my hands busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big risk and the people in charge should be honest about it. I'd say families should start talking now, kitchen table first. At church I'd ask the elders for their view, because they've seen big changes before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would worry me, but I'd also feel strangely focused. By 2028, anything done on a screen is doing what a person does. Robots for hands-on work arrive around 2031, so my repair and installation skills would still have a few years. After that, nothing is certain. I'd rather admit I don't know than act like I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the shop job full-time right away, because it's income and hands-on. I'd build a repair-and-install business around it, with my uncle's licence and my own name. I'd keep my savings steady, and I'd put any spare money into tools and stock rather than shares. And I'd start learning how to service robots and sensor systems, since someone will have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be thinking about my grandmother and my parents, and how my family's savings would hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather admit you don't know. Is that hard for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'm the one in the family people ask about tech. If I say I don't know, they look worried. But a bluff would be worse. My grandmother says honesty is a kind of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why tools and stock rather than shares?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can touch them and use them. A shop with tools can earn if the economy wobbles. Shares can vanish on a Tuesday. I'm not against shares, I'm just not sure what I'd be buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if we get on with it. I'd tell people to work, save and learn something that matters. At home I'd say we have time to do this properly, as a family, and make a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be hopeful. In five years I could have a good engineering job, a few years of experience, and a business started. Robots for hands-on work around 2034 means my shop skills would still earn for a while. I'd say I'd be in better shape than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take an engineering job in the first six months and keep the shop work on Saturdays. I'd save 500 a month, and I'd buy a small flat with my cousin as an investment. I'd study an evening course on electrical safety standards, since that's a job that needs people. And I'd use AI for the routine design checks, once my firm approves it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with some drive in it. Five years feels like enough for me to build something I own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a flat with your cousin. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd each put in a deposit of about 8,000 and rent it to students. It's a small thing, but it's real. My father always says own what you can. I'd read the lease twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family at home about a plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write it on the back of an envelope, three lines. Job, savings, shop. My grandmother likes a plan she can read at the table. She'd put it behind the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough to build a life. I'd say we should still be careful, because tech companies like to promise things. At church I'd say, remember to keep looking after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel good. By 2036 I'd be thirty-three, with a career, a family maybe, and a business. Robots for hands-on work are in 2039, so even more time. If I'm sensible, I'd have a home paid down and savings. The one worry is that people stop learning because they think there's plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work at an engineering firm for three years, then decide whether to go on my own with the shop. I'd marry in the middle somewhere, ideally, and buy a house. I'd learn the AI tools as they come to my work. I'd also mentor a younger lad from church who wants to do electronics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, definitely. It's the kind of timeline where I'd sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would the lad from church be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His name's Elijah. He's fifteen and keeps taking radios apart. I'd lend him a soldering iron and a few old boards. Somebody did that for me, my uncle, and I never forgot it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean to go on your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have my name above the door and a van. I'd do installs, repairs and some design work. If it goes badly, I'd go back to a firm. I'd rather try at twenty-six than wonder at forty.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. It's too fast for families to adjust, and my family's savings aren't huge. What would help is real apprenticeships, tax breaks for small firms that take on young engineers, and honest talk from tech companies about what they're building.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say that people don't give my generation enough credit for wanting to work. We want a job that's ours. We just need someone to give us a first chance.

headlineQuote: People don't give my generation enough credit for wanting to work. We want a job that's ours.
portrait: Jamal is **23**, an electronic engineering graduate with a pass, living in Nottingham with family and working at his uncle's repair shop.
He is traditional and pro-business: he likes **ownership**, apprenticeships and family backing over public help.
He is a steady adopter who uses AI **now and then**, checks every number, and waits for proof first.
His hands-on **shop experience** makes him calmer than most, and he reaches anxious only in the 2028 world.
He wants a place that is **his own**, whether at a firm first or through his own business at twenty-six.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most because it is too fast for families to adjust and his savings are modest.
whatWouldHelp: Real **apprenticeships**, tax breaks for small firms that hire young engineers, and honest talk from tech companies.
